report.answer_text:
Baby KJ Muldoon received a personalised CRISPR-based base-editing therapy for a rare metabolic disease called carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1) deficiency. The case was reported in May 2025 in the *New England Journal of Medicine* and presented at the American Society of Gene & Cell Therapy meeting.
The condition: CPS1 deficiency prevents the liver from clearing ammonia, which can cause brain damage or death. The usual treatments are a severely restricted protein diet, medication, and eventually a liver transplant.
The therapy: The treatment was a bespoke base editor, often called "k-abe". It was designed to correct the single-letter DNA mutation in KJ's *CPS1* gene. Base editing changes one DNA letter without cutting both strands of the DNA.
Delivery: The editing machinery was packaged in lipid nanoparticles, which carry it to the liver. It was given by intravenous infusion.
Who made it: The team was led by doctors at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and Penn Medicine, including Kiran Musunuru and Rebecca Ahrens-Nicklas. They worked with partners including Danaher, Aldevron, IDT and Acuitas. The therapy was designed, made and approved in about six months.
Dosing: KJ got three doses in total, starting at around 6 months old. The first was in February 2025, and the later doses followed in the next weeks. Several doses were given because the lipid nanoparticle delivery allows re-dosing, unlike viral vectors.
Early results: He tolerated the treatment without serious side effects. He was able to eat more protein and needed less nitrogen-scavenging medication, and he coped better with common childhood illnesses. The team said it was too early to call it a cure and that long-term follow-up is needed.
The case is widely seen as a proof of concept for on-demand, individualised gene-editing treatments for very rare genetic diseases.
